articles.title: SkyStriker a big hit at Yudh Abhyas 2026: Inside India's precision loitering munition
articles.summary: The SkyStriker loitering munition carried out a precision strike at the Mahajan Field Firing Range during the ongoing India-US military exercise Yudh
articles.body: The SkyStriker loitering munition carried out a precision strike at the Mahajan Field Firing Range during the ongoing India-US military exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, demonstrating the system's ability to detect, engage and accurately hit designated targets in a realistic operational setting.The Indian Army's demonstration highlighted the growing role of indigenous defence technology, unmanned systems and precision-strike capabilities in modern warfare, according to news agency ANI.Yudh Abhyas 2026 is focused on enhancing interoperability between Indian and US forces, with troops training alongside drones, autonomous systems and other emerging battlefield technologies. The exercise is also aimed at preparing both armies for increasingly technology-driven combat environments.SkyStriker & its key features and capabilitiesThe SkyStriker is a loitering munition, an unmanned weapon system that combines surveillance, target acquisition and precision strike capabilities.It can be launched to search for a designated target, remain airborne over an area and then engage the target when directed.The system was developed by Israel-based Elbit Systems and is manufactured in India through its partnership with Bengaluru-based Alpha Design Technologies.The SkyStriker can carry either a 5-kg or 10-kg warhead and uses electric propulsion, allowing it to operate with a relatively low acoustic signature.According to Elbit Systems, the system can travel up to 20 km in about 10 minutes and can remain airborne for up to two hours with a 5-kg warhead or one hour with a 10-kg warhead.For target acquisition, the loitering munition is equipped with a gimballed dual CCD and infrared seeker, along with a synchronised dual tracker. It can dive towards its target at speeds of up to 300 knots.The system also features autonomous navigation during its cruise and loitering phases, as well as abort, go-around and re-engagement capabilities.The SkyStriker was also used operationally during Operation Sindoor in May 2025, when the Indian armed forces carried out strikes against terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir.

articles.title: ‘Mobilizing myth’: Why is Russia sending dead princes, saints into Ukraine battle
articles.summary: Russian troops fighting in eastern Ukraine are receiving an unusual form of support as the war enters another winter.
articles.body: Russian troops fighting in eastern Ukraine are receiving an unusual form of support as the war enters another winter. Relics of medieval Russian rulers and warrior saints are being taken to military bases and units at the front.In early September, a fragment of the remains of Dmitry Donskoy, the Moscow prince celebrated for his victory at the 1380 Battle of Kulikovo, was sent to Russian troops and is now being moved around military bases in Russian-occupied Ukraine. The relic is a fragment of his right hand, the same hand the Russian Orthodox Church says he used to wield his sword in battle.The military department of the Moscow Patriarchate said the “saint commander” would invisibly stand “shoulder to shoulder” with Russian soldiers. The move is part of a broader role the Russian Orthodox Church has played during the war, with religious symbolism being used alongside state narratives about Russia’s military campaign, according to a CNN report.“The church has practically merged with the state to the point of being indistinguishable,” the report quoted Sergei Chapnin saying, a religious scholar and director of communications at Fordham University’s Orthodox Christian Studies Center. “From my point of view, the maximum (closeness) has been reached.”Why Donskoy’s relics were taken to the frontThe practice of taking sacred relics to troops is not new in Orthodox Christianity. But experts say Donskoy’s medieval military legacy gives the relic a particular significance in the context of the Ukraine war.Chapnin said Donskoy is presented not as an aggressor but as a defender of his homeland, allowing the historical figure to be linked to Russia’s present-day narrative about the war.“He was not himself an aggressor, but a defender of the fatherland,” the scholar told CNN. From the government’s perspective, “it is very important to show that Russia is not the aggressor, that we are defending our territory.”Chapnin described this connection between Russia’s medieval past and its current war as “a mobilizing myth.”“These myths, which connect different times and eras, can act quite powerfully on mass consciousness,” he said, adding that the relics are presented as “a magical artifact.”Metropolitan Vladimir, the Russian-installed Orthodox leader in Donetsk and Mariupol, said the relic would help soldiers and civilians “mobilize both their spiritual and physical strength” and “triumph over the enemy.”Donskoy is not the only medieval Russian ruler whose relics have been taken to the war zone. Earlier this year, relics of Prince Alexander Nevsky, another ruler later turned into a symbol of Russian military glory, were also taken to troops.From Kremlin to Church, a closer wartime relationshipThe use of religious relics comes against the backdrop of a closer relationship between the Kremlin and the Russian Orthodox Church since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.The Church has repeatedly used religious language to support Russia’s military narrative. The recovery of Donskoy’s remains in August was itself given religious and historical significance by Russia’s political and religious leadership.President Vladimir Putin called the recovery an “absolutely unique” and “marvelous discovery”, while Patriarch Kirill described it as “a special sign of God’s providence.”The relics have also been displayed in Moscow, where thousands participated in religious events involving Donskoy’s remains. An annual religious procession in September drew more than 100,000 people in Moscow alone, according to official figures.But the role of the Church in the war has drawn criticism from within the wider Orthodox community.For Rev Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian, the use of Donskoy’s remains “has nothing to do with Christianity.”“It is undoubtedly the exploitation of Christianity and the exploitation of the church for ‘patriotic’ purposes," CNN quoted him saying. He argued that the Church’s strong state backing creates incentives to align with the Kremlin, calling the use of the remains a “cynical calculation.”What soldiers make of itThe religious symbolism does not necessarily have the same meaning for troops at the front.Some Russian soldiers say faith has become more important as the war continues. A former Russian serviceman told CNN that soldiers often turn to God during difficult moments.“Not all of us talk to God when things are going well, but everyone talks to God when things are bad,” he said.He described makeshift churches at the front, soldiers praying before missions and priests visiting military units and hospitals.“Like a field kitchen, there should be a priest everywhere,” he said, quoting a popular Russian expression: “We are Russians. God is with us.”A Russian soldier serving in the Zaporizhzhia region described being able to speak to a priest, pray or touch a holy object as “serious moral support.”But not all soldiers see the relics as meaningful.One serviceman in the Donbas region called the decision to send them to the front “a very unconventional solution to our problems in the 21st century.”“My view is that they are needed more by the mothers of the guys who died in this military operation,” he added.The war has also raised questions within the Orthodox community over the role priests should play in supporting soldiers. Rev Grigory Mikhnov-Vaytenko, a Russian priest who helps Ukrainian refugees displaced by the war, said spiritual support should not become a means of reinforcing an illusion about the conflict.“We need to support people, including those in military uniform,” he said. “But the question is how we support them.”“On the one hand, (you must) not deny people spiritual help, and on the other, not lead them into an illusion,” CNN quoted the priest as saying.The debate comes as the war enters its fifth year, with Russian soldiers describing mounting strain at the front. For the Kremlin and the Russian Orthodox Church, however, the medieval warrior saints and their relics offer a way to connect Russia’s military present with its religious and historical past.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2002, Scotland opened the Falkirk Wheel to lift boats 100 feet between canals, replacing 11 locks with a rotating 1,800-tonne structure
articles.summary: Opened in 2002, the Falkirk Wheel transformed how boats travel between two historic canals in central Scotland.
articles.body: Opened in 2002, the Falkirk Wheel transformed how boats travel between two historic canals in central Scotland. The rotating boat lift connects the Forth and Clyde Canal with the Union Canal, which lies about 100 feet higher. Instead of relying on the former flight of 11 locks, the structure uses two water-filled gondolas that rotate to raise and lower vessels. The system was designed to keep the gondolas balanced, allowing the 1,800-tonne structure to operate using just 1.5 kWh for each rotation, according to Scottish Canals. The energy used is commonly compared with that required to boil eight kettles.How the Falkirk Wheel replaced 11 locks with a rotating boat liftThe Falkirk Wheel was built as part of efforts to restore the Forth and Clyde Canal and the Union Canal. The Forth and Clyde Canal was built in 1790, while the Union Canal opened in 1822. The two waterways had originally been connected at Falkirk through a series of 11 locks, but the locks later became unusable, and the canals were eventually closed.The restoration project sought a new way to connect the waterways rather than simply rebuilding the old staircase of locks. The Linda Hall Library says British Waterways Scotland worked with architectural and engineering firms to develop a unique boat-lift design. The resulting structure uses two gondolas positioned on opposite sides of the rotating wheel, allowing boats to be raised and lowered as the wheel turns.How the Falkirk Wheel raises boats 100 feet between two Scottish canalsEach side of the Falkirk Wheel contains a gondola capable of carrying canal boats. The Linda Hall Library states that each gondola can accommodate up to four canal boats, or one or two larger boats. Once the boats enter, seals are raised to make the gondolas watertight, and the wheel rotates to exchange their positions. Scottish Canals similarly describes the Wheel as connecting the two canals 35 metres above.How the Falkirk Wheel uses 1.5 kWh to rotate its 1,800-tonne structureA central feature of the design is the balance between the two gondolas. The two gondolas, when full of water, weigh the same regardless of how many boats they contain. It attributes this to Archimedes’ principle: when a boat enters a full gondola, it displaces water equal to its own weight, leaving the total weight unchanged.According to Scottish Canals, the structure weighs 1,800 tonnes and uses just 1.5 kWh for each rotation. The Linda Hall Library gives a figure of about 1.5 kilowatt-hours for one half-turn and notes the commonly cited comparison that this is about the same amount of energy required to boil eight kettles of water.How the Falkirk Wheel cut a full-day canal journey to just a few minutesBefore the Wheel was built, vessels travelling between the two canals had to pass through the former flight of 11 locks. Scottish Canals says this meant opening and closing 44 lock gates and could take a full day. The Wheel reduced the canal transfer to a journey of only a few minutes.Since opening, the Falkirk Wheel has also become a major visitor destination. Scottish Canals says it attracts around 500,000 visitors each year and describes it as one of Scotland's busiest tourist attractions. The organisation calls it a "working sculpture" combining modern engineering and technology with principles associated with Archimedes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Brazil restored river forests using three seeding methods and planted seedlings; 15 years later, row-seeding stored 155 tonnes of biomass per hectare
articles.summary: Since 2006, researchers working with the Instituto Socioambiental have restored 75 riparian forest sites along a 500km stretch of Mato Grosso, Brazil,
articles.body: Since 2006, researchers working with the Instituto Socioambiental have restored 75 riparian forest sites along a 500km stretch of Mato Grosso, Brazil, using five different approaches, three direct seeding techniques (broadcast, hole and row), seedling planting, and natural regeneration. Fifteen years on, a study published in the Journal of Environmental Management found the results were far from equal. Row-seeding, in particular, pulled dramatically ahead of every other method for storing carbon above ground. Here's how a simple choice in planting technique ended up making such an outsized difference.A 15-year experiment across 75 riparian forests in BrazilThe study ‘Carbon stocks in riparian forests in the Amazonia-Cerrado transition over 15 years: Effects of restoration methods and edaphoclimatic factors’ tracked 75 sites in the Amazonia-Cerrado transition zone, all previously cleared for cattle pasture, sampling each one in 2017 and again in 2022 as part of a continuous 15-year chronosequence. Sites were restored using broadcast-seeding (45 sites), hole-seeding (11), row-seeding (10), seedling planting (4) or natural regeneration (5). By the 15-year mark, row-seeding had produced a mean aboveground biomass of 155.2 tonnes per hectare, roughly double that of broadcast-seeding (80.6 tonnes) and hole-seeding (73.8 tonnes), and well ahead of seedling planting (67.8 tonnes) and even natural regeneration (97.1 tonnes).Why row-seeding grew bigger trees than broadcasting or holesThe researchers traced row-seeding's advantage to the mechanical precision of the grain drills used to plant it, which buried seeds at a depth well suited to certain long-lived pioneer species. Chief among them was Enterolobium timbouva, an oval-seeded tree with substantial energy reserves that can emerge from deeper soil, protected from predators and drying out, and which came to dominate row-seeded sites older than a decade. By contrast, broadcast-seeding favoured Tachigali vulgaris, a small-seeded species that thrives near the surface but tends to die off within 10 to 20 years, helping explain why broadcast sites' biomass growth slowed over time as that transitory species was replaced.The hidden divide; carbon in trees vs carbon in soilWhile the trees above ground told a clear story of technique mattering enormously, the carbon stored in the soil beneath told a completely different one. Soil organic carbon stocks, ranging from 11.4 to 73.5 tonnes per hectare across all sites, showed no meaningful link to a site's age or its restoration method at all. Instead, soil carbon was shaped almost entirely by local conditions such as cation exchange capacity, base saturation and moisture, meaning restoration choices that dramatically boost trees overhead may do little to change what's stored underground, a decoupling the researchers say reflects patterns seen elsewhere in tropical forest research.Row-seeding's cost advantage for carbon-focused restorationBeyond its ecological edge, row-seeding also came out ahead financially. It cost roughly $2,442 per hectare to implement, similar to broadcast-seeding (2,451) and was cheaper than hole-seeding ($3,246), yet its far greater carbon capture meant it worked out to just $7.91 per tonne of CO2 sequestered over 15 years, compared with $15.30 for broadcast and $22.10 for hole-seeding. That makes row-seeding not just the most effective of the three direct-seeding techniques studied, but also one of the more cost-effective restoration strategies documented anywhere in the tropics, well below the roughly $29 per tonne reported for mixed-species tree plantings elsewhere in Brazil.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bangladesh jewellery shop owner's body found inside floating drum; Hindu credit union token in pocket
articles.summary: The body of a 50-year-old jewellery shop owner found stuffed inside a drum floating near a sluice gate in Bangladesh's Mymensingh has been identified,
articles.body: The body of a 50-year-old jewellery shop owner found stuffed inside a drum floating near a sluice gate in Bangladesh's Mymensingh has been identified, police said.The body was recovered on Wednesday after local residents spotted a drum floating in the water near the sluice gate in the Begunbari area. Police found the body of an unidentified man wrapped in cloth inside the drum.A token belonging to Mymensingh Hindu Cooperative Credit Union Limited was found in the trouser pocket of the body. Police contacted the organisation using the token, which helped establish the man's identity as Niranjan Chandra Sutradhar, who ran a jointly owned jewellery shop in the Atharbari Building area of Mymensingh city.Niranjan's wife, Sumita Rani Sutradhar, and son, Joy Sutradhar, identified his body on Thursday evening.Kotwali Model Police Station Sub-Inspector Ruhul Amin said, "After receiving the token, the Mymensingh Hindu Cooperative Credit Union Limited was contacted. The people of the institution helped identify Niranjan after seeing the token. Later, his identity was confirmed by contacting the family," as quoted by Bangladesh's Daily Ittefaq newspaper.Niranjan lived with his wife and son in a rented house in the Stadium area. He went missing on September 20, but his family did not file a general diary as he had previously stayed away from home for three to four days before returning.Police said the body had sharp-weapon injury marks on the head and chest. Kotwali Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge Muhammad Shibirul Islam said, "It is initially believed that Niranjan was killed and his body was thrown into the water after being placed in a drum."Police have not yet established who killed Niranjan or the motive in initial probe. No one had been arrested as of Friday morning.A case had not been registered as of Thursday night, with police saying the process of filing a complaint on behalf of the family was under way.You use AI every day. articles.title: The learning crisis: When schooling does not become learning
articles.summary: This is a real instance from my time as a school principal.
articles.body: This is a real instance from my time as a school principal. Although it happened decades ago, the student’s helplessness and our inability to help him still trouble me. The student was a cheerful, confident and articulate student, fluent in languages, well informed, and passionate about innovations in science and technology. He represented the school in several competitions, led the assembly and was a member of the prefect council. Why, then, did his mathematics grades keep falling with every successive class? By the time he reached Class X, his teachers, parents, tutors and school were unable to find an effective way to help him. His continuing struggle eroded his cheer and self-confidence, leaving him increasingly stressed and discouraged. Eventually, he could not clear the mathematics board examination.His experience raises a fundamental question: how are schooling and learning different? Schooling provides the curriculum, timetable and opportunity. Learning is the process through which children develop knowledge, understanding and skills—and become capable of using them independently. A school can report strong examination results, completed syllabi and successful promotions while some children continue to struggle with essential concepts. The institutional picture may appear reassuring; the individual learner’s experience may be very different from it.The learning crisis begins wherever schooling fails to develop understanding that children can apply independently, including in unfamiliar situations. It may affect many students, a small group or a single learner. For each child affected, persistent difficulty can become a personal crisis, weakening confidence, participation and the willingness to persevere.National findings support the concern. ASER 2024 found that more than half of Class V children in rural India could not read a Class II-level text, despite improvement since 2022. PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024 reported an average mathematics score of 39 per cent among Class IX students in recognised private schools of India. The surveys invite schools to examine their own evidence. Children are progressing through classes; is their learning progressing with them?When a learning gap becomes a learning debtConsider a student who calculates percentages correctly but cannot explain why a twenty per cent discount followed by another ten per cent discount is not equivalent to thirty per cent off. The student knows the procedure but struggles to apply the concept in a different situation. Classroom learning may have remained confined to familiar exercises.A learning gap is a gap in the knowledge, understanding or skills needed at a particular stage. If a child has not understood fractions, learning percentages, ratios and algebra may become difficult. An unresolved gap can grow into a learning debt: each new topic builds on concepts the learner has not yet understood, making it increasingly difficult to catch up.Completed notebooks, polished projects and satisfactory report cards can conceal this difficulty. Principals need a clear process that connects institutional priorities with individual progress: making learning the priority, identifying difficulties, providing support and checking each learner’s progress. These four steps offer school principals a practical roadmap.1. Establish learning as the institutional priorityThe questions a principal asks in academic reviews communicate what the school values. Questions about syllabus completion, results and promotion remain useful but must be accompanied by questions about learning and understanding.What have students learned? Can they apply it independently? What evidence demonstrates this? Who needs support, and when will its effectiveness be reviewed?Meetings should conclude with specific decisions, clearly assigned responsibilities and review dates.2. Identify specific gaps through evidenceClear learning outcomes are essential at every level in every subject. What should students understand, what should they be able to do, and what would demonstrate that capability? Competency-based learning translates these questions into purposeful classroom tasks. Students expected to reason need opportunities to explain their reasoning. Those expected to apply knowledge need appropriate opportunities to use it beyond familiar exercises.In language, students interpret an unfamiliar passage and support their interpretation with evidence from the text.In science, students predict what changing one condition in an experiment might do and explain why.In social science, students compare two accounts of an event and explain how their perspectives differ.In each case, students provide evidence of learning through what they explain, justify or apply. A correct answer may follow a memorised procedure; asking students to explain their answer can reveal whether they understand the concept.Diagnostic assessment helps locate learning gaps. For example, a low mathematics score alone cannot show whether the problem concerns number understanding, language, method or a prerequisite concept. Brief questions, classroom tasks and discussions can provide useful evidence that will reveal the gap in understanding. Quality of assessment depends on the thinking it requires. Contrary to the popular belief a lengthy case study may test recall; a short question may reveal a misconception.Evidence must also lead to a decision about the support for students. If several students share a misconception, teaching may need revision. If the difficulty is individual, support can be targeted.3. Organise support that addresses the difficultyIdentification must lead to a planned response for learner support. Just extra practice cannot reliably resolve learning gaps that were developed in earlier grades. Some learners need a concept to be retaught, others require focused practice, and some need individual attention. School Principals must establish what support will be provided, by whom and when.Teachers require relevant professional development, resources and time for peer-collaboration. Examining student work together can help them compare explanations and refine their approaches.Professional trust between school leadership and teachers matters equally. Can a teacher acknowledge that several children in the class have not understood a concept and expect guidance rather than blame? A constructive response makes it easier for teachers to report difficulties early and seek help.4. Review progress and adjust the responseProviding support is an activity. Improved understanding is the intended outcome. Academic reviews should revisit earlier decisions and examine their effects. This continuity makes follow-up an institutional practice and recognises progress that may otherwise escape attention. After the support is given, it is important to return to the original learning goal and review the students’ performance.Schooling is the process. Learning is the purpose. Every learner’s progress is the school’s responsibility.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: When the referee fumbles: Election Commission row explained in 7 key questions
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Elections are, by their very nature, a contest.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Elections are, by their very nature, a contest.Political parties fight for ground, candidates wage fierce campaigns and voters ultimately decide whom to trust with their mandate.Through it all, the Election Commission is meant to stand apart and monitor the process. Its role is to frame the rules, enforce them fairly and ensure that the contest remains even-handed.Yet, in recent days, the spotlight has moved away from those fighting the election and towards the institution meant to referee it.The players are no longer the only ones under scrutiny. Increasingly, the referee itself has become the subject of the debate.A report in The Indian Express claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi repeatedly raised objections with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over decisions and communications that they said were issued without their knowledge or approval.The Election Commission has rejected the suggestion that the episode points to a breakdown in its functioning. It has maintained that differences of opinion are a normal part of institutional deliberation and that all final decisions of the Commission have been unanimous.That leaves a larger constitutional question at the heart of the controversy: how is India's election watchdog actually supposed to function?Is the Chief Election Commissioner the boss of the Election Commission, or simply the first among three equals? What happens when the three commissioners disagree? And why has the law governing their appointment become a subject of such intense controversy?What triggered the latest EC controversy?On September 23, The Indian Express reported that Sandhu and Joshi had, on multiple occasions, objected to decisions and communications they said were taken or issued without their prior knowledge.According to the report, the two commissioners recorded such objections on at least 14 occasions over the past 10 months.The issues reportedly ranged from changes to electoral forms and access to the voter database to the allocation of work within the Commission and the filing of appeals involving electoral rolls.The report has since triggered a wider debate over whether the Election Commission's three members are exercising their powers collectively, as the law envisages, or whether the CEC has acquired a greater role in practice.What did the two ECs object to?According to the Indian Express report, the concerns raised by Sandhu and Joshi covered several aspects of the Commission's functioning.Changes to Form 6: The two commissioners reportedly objected to changes made to Form 6, the application citizens use to register as new electors, without following due process. In May, Joshi warned that the form could not be altered without an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. On August 13, Sandhu reportedly described the change as "unauthorised and illegal" and called for its immediate removal.Access to electoral roll data: The commissioners also reportedly raised concerns about whether statutory authorities responsible for maintaining electoral rolls had complete access to voter data on the ERONet portal. Joshi flagged what he described as the "gradual centralisation of the electoral roll database" and proposed an audit to establish that only authorised officials had credentials to modify voter data. Sandhu, separately, recorded that state-level election officials had complained of not having "proper and complete access" to ERONet. He also questioned whether the Commission's director general of IT, Seema Khanna, had the legal authority to restrict access for statutory officials such as Electoral Registration Officers.Changes in work allocation: Joshi and Sandhu reportedly wrote separately to the cabinet secretary objecting to changes in the allocation of work that removed a layer of oversight over the Commission's IT infrastructure. They said the changes had been made without their knowledge.West Bengal SIR appeals: During the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in West Bengal, the Election Commission filed around 16.10 lakh appeals involving voters whose names judicial officers had added. The appeals were heard by tribunals headed by retired high court judges appointed by the Supreme Court. According to the report, neither the two election commissioners nor West Bengal's chief electoral officer were informed about the basis or process for filing these appeals.Restoration of voters in Goa: Another concern reportedly involved 97 eligible voters whose names had to be restored to Goa's electoral rolls. Despite repeated requests from Electoral Registration Officers, the voters could not initially be restored because the ECI's software did not have an option for reinstatement.Communications issued in the ECI's name: The two commissioners also reportedly objected to communications being issued in the Election Commission's name without what they considered to be the Commission's full approval. They cited Article 324 of the Constitution as well as the 2023 law governing the poll panel.Taken together, the reported objections raise a question that goes beyond any individual decision: how does a three-member constitutional body exercise collective authority when its members do not initially agree?What did the Election Commission say?The Election Commission strongly rejected the suggestion that its internal differences amount to a breakdown in decision-making, and added that all official orders and administrative directions had been issued unanimously."Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the ECI said in a statement."In recent months, the Commission has taken numerous decisions, issued instructions, introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms, including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year," the poll body added.It also criticised the media report, saying that highlighting specific internal notes over a period of 10 months gives only one part of the picture."Highlighting certain specific internal notes/observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives give only one part of the picture," it said.The disagreement, therefore, is not simply over whether commissioners have expressed reservations. It is over what those reservations mean for the functioning of the institution as a whole.CEC or ECs: Who has the final say?This is where the 2023 law becomes important.Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, provides that the Commission may, by unanimous decision, regulate how its business is conducted and allocate work among the CEC and the other Election Commissioners.It also says that, as far as possible, the Commission's business should be transacted unanimously.But it makes an important provision for situations in which consensus is not possible.If the CEC and the other Election Commissioners differ on a matter, the issue is to be decided according to the opinion of the majority.In other words, the statutory framework does not make the CEC an executive superior to the other two commissioners. The three constitute the Commission collectively, while the CEC is the "first among equals".The CEC can have a distinct role within the institution, but the law does not provide for a system in which the CEC's view automatically prevails over the other two commissioners.Where the three disagree, the majority view is the deciding view.The controversy now centres on whether some of the decisions cited in the recent report were, in practice, implemented despite objections from the other two commissioners, and if so, how that squares with the statutory scheme governing the Commission's decision-making.Why is the 2023 EC law controversial?The current controversy also brings back an older and deeper question: Who should appoint the people who conduct India's elections?In March 2023, the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament had not yet enacted a law governing appointments to the Election Commission, despite Article 324 of the Constitution envisaging such a framework.Until Parliament enacted such a law, a Constitution bench prescribed an interim selection mechanism comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India.The court stressed that an independent Election Commission was essential for democracy and observed that those entrusted with conducting elections must be insulated from executive influence.Parliament subsequently enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.But the new law changed the composition of the selection committee.Instead of the Chief Justice of India, it provided for a Union Cabinet minister nominated by the Prime Minister. The committee therefore consists of the Prime Minister, a Union minister nominated by him and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.The opposition has alleged that the 2023 Act gives the executive “overwhelming” control over the appointment of Election Commissioners. The government, meanwhile, has defended the law and its institutional framework.Matter in Supreme CourtThe dispute has now reached the Supreme Court, where a challenge to the validity of the appointment law produced a split verdict.A two-judge SC bench differed over whether the matter should immediately be referred to a Constitution bench. Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma disagreed on that question, although both agreed that the matter should ultimately be placed before the Chief Justice of India for consideration by a larger bench.They also agreed that sending the case first to a three-judge bench would be of "little worth" and could further delay a final determination of the constitutional questions involved. The matter is likely to be heard by a 5-judge bench soon.The issue is vital as it extends beyond the current dispute inside the Election Commission. It touches a larger institutional question: How independent should the body conducting India's elections be from the executive, and what safeguards should govern the appointment of those who head it?Can a CEC actually be removed?The latest controversy has also acquired a political dimension, with opposition parties preparing fresh notices seeking the removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.According to media reports, the notices, being drafted and vetted by experts, are expected to be submitted in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha next week. The proposed notices are expected to include issues raised in the Indian Express report.This would not be the opposition's first attempt.On April 7, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairperson CP Radhakrishnan rejected an earlier notice seeking Kumar's removal. That notice had been signed by 130 Lok Sabha members and 63 Rajya Sabha members and alleged partisanship and arbitrariness in the conduct of the SIR exercise.Separately, a notice submitted by 73 opposition MPs in the Rajya Sabha on April 24 seeking Kumar's removal remains pending in the Upper House.But removing a CEC is deliberately difficult.Article 324(5) of the Constitution provides that the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only "in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court".The same protection is incorporated into Section 11(2) of the 2023 Act.The other Election Commissioners enjoy a different safeguard: they cannot be removed from office except on the recommendation of the CEC.The higher threshold for removing a CEC is intended to protect the office from arbitrary or politically motivated removal.What does it take to remove a CEC?The removal process is rooted in the constitutional procedure applicable to Supreme Court judges.Article 124(4) of the Constitution, which lays down the procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge, states that a judge can be removed only by an order of the President following an address by each House of Parliament.Such an address must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of at least two-thirds of members present and voting, in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.The process begins with a notice of motion in either House of Parliament alleging misbehaviour or incapacity. The notice must be signed by at least 100 MPs in the Lok Sabha or 50 MPs in the Rajya Sabha.The presiding officer of the concerned House can admit or refuse the motion after considering the material and information available. If the motion is admitted, an inquiry is conducted into the charges by a committee constituted for the purpose.If the charges are established, the motion must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in both Houses.Once both Houses pass the motion in accordance with these requirements, an address is made to the President, who then issues the order removing the CEC.The President's role at this stage is constitutional and formal once Parliament has passed the required address.How the EC evolvedThe current structure of the Election Commission is itself the product of an institutional evolution.When the ECI was established in 1950, it was a single-member body, with the Chief Election Commissioner as its sole member.It became a three-member body for the first time in 1989, but that arrangement was short-lived. In January 1990, the VP Singh government reverted the Commission to a single-member structure.The system changed again in October 1993, when the PV Narasimha Rao government appointed MS Gill and GVG Krishnamurthy as Election Commissioners alongside CEC TN Seshan.Seshan challenged the appointments in the Supreme Court, arguing that the addition of commissioners diluted the authority of the CEC.In its 1995 judgment, a Constitution bench upheld the multi-member structure.The court made clear that the CEC was not institutionally superior to the other Election Commissioners. The three were intended to function collectively, with differences being resolved through the decision-making mechanism of the Commission.That judgment established the broad institutional framework that exists today.The big pictureThe Election Commission is not designed as a hierarchy in which one person commands and two others merely assist. Nor is it simply three independent offices operating in parallel. It is a constitutional body meant to function collectively.The law provides for unanimity where possible and a majority where consensus fails.The CEC occupies the position of first among equals, rather than that of a superior authority.The significance of the current controversy, therefore, lies not merely in the existence of disagreements within the Commission. Differences are inevitable in any institution exercising such enormous constitutional responsibility.The larger question is what happens after those differences arise: whether they remain part of an internal deliberative process, as the ECI maintains, or whether they reflect a deeper dispute over how collective authority is being exercised.The credibility of an election does not rest only on the final tally of votes.It also rests on whether voters believe that the rules were applied fairly, the institutions enforcing them remained above the contest and the process was conducted without favour or hidden influence.The Election Commission, therefore, carries a burden that goes beyond administering polls: it must command confidence across the political spectrum and among voters themselves. Any perception that the referee is divided, opaque or partisan can cast a shadow over the process, even when the electoral machinery continues to function formally within the law.In the end, public trust is not built merely by declaring an election free and fair; it is built by ensuring that voters have little reason to doubt that verdict.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Committed to protecting students' right to protest': CJI Surya Kant at Patna law university event
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Saturday asserted that the judiciary would not “look the other way” when students’ fundamental right
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant on Saturday asserted that the judiciary would not “look the other way” when students’ fundamental right to hold peaceful protests is "infringed."The CJI made the remarks during an “unfiltered interaction” with students at Chanakya National Law University (CNLU) in Patna. According to a university statement, he told the students that he preferred a "frank question-and-answer session."During the interaction, a student asked the CJI about the “police response to peaceful students’ protests”.According to the statement, CJI Kant told the student that “courts will not look the other way” in cases involving alleged police brutality. He also “unequivocally reaffirmed the judiciary’s commitment to protecting students’ peaceful right to protest."The reference was to the Jantar Mantar protests in Delhi against the NEET exam paper leaks, spearheaded by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), a youth pressure group. The CJP began as a satirical online campaign following the CJI’s “cockroaches” remark in the Supreme Court, which he later clarified had been reported out of context.A CJP-called march to Parliament on July 20 ended in clashes between protesters and Delhi Police and other security forces. The protests were called off on July 25 after then-Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned, fulfilling the CJP’s principal demand. The group had also sought an assurance that no student who participated in the demonstrations would be booked.On September 1, a CJI-led bench quashed the FIRs registered in connection with the July 20 clashes after the Centre and state governments assured the Supreme Court that cases against the protesters would not be pursued and no fresh FIRs would be registered over the same incidents.The order, however, does not apply to 2,873 people with criminal backgrounds who were identified at the Jantar Mantar demonstrations.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2019, three Pennsylvania investors paid $100,000 for an abandoned high school; after an 18-month, roughly $3.3 million conversion, its classrooms became 31 apartments that reached full occupancy within six months
articles.summary: A high school that sat empty for years is now home to dozens of people, after three Pennsylvania investors turned its old classrooms into apartments.
articles.body: A high school that sat empty for years is now home to dozens of people, after three Pennsylvania investors turned its old classrooms into apartments. In 2019, three friends bought an abandoned school building in Homestead, Pennsylvania, for just $100,000. What followed was far more expensive than the purchase price. Over the next 18 months, they spent roughly $3.3 million transforming the former school into a 31-unit apartment building. The project involved gutting and rebuilding much of the interior while keeping some of the features that made the building recognisable as a school. In interviews with CNBC Make It, the investors detailed how they took on the unusual conversion and eventually filled all 31 apartments within six months of opening them for rent.The $100,000 building that needed a new purposeThe property had been sitting vacant for years when the three investors, Jesse Wig, Adam Colucci and Dan Spanovich, purchased it. Rather than starting with a traditional apartment building, they were dealing with a former high school that had already seen better days. The partners initially considered several different uses for the building. According to CNBC Make It, ideas included turning it into a co-working space, a concert venue or a beer garden. They eventually decided that converting it into housing offered the most practical use for the property.The building had around 55,000 square feet of space, although only about 20,000 square feet was ultimately available for leasing because of the building’s large hallways, staircases, gym and auditorium. The $100,000 purchase price also turned out to be only the beginning. The renovation ultimately cost approximately $3.3 million, turning a relatively inexpensive property acquisition into a major redevelopment project.Classrooms were rebuilt as apartmentsThe investors did not simply divide the old school into identical rental units. The renovation involved rebuilding the former classrooms as modern apartments while retaining several details from the building's past. The completed property has 31 apartments, including one- and two-bedroom units. Former classrooms were converted into living spaces with kitchens and bathrooms, while features such as the building's high ceilings and large windows helped give the apartments a distinctive character.Some of the old school features were deliberately kept rather than removed. Original chalkboards remain in some apartments, providing an obvious reminder of what the rooms were once used for. The building's shared spaces also received new purposes. The former auditorium, for example, was restored rather than simply stripped out. The renovation preserved parts of its original character while turning it into a communal area for residents.The gymnasium was given another life as well. The old basketball court was retained, while the space was adapted into a fitness area. Instead of becoming unusable remnants of an abandoned school, these large spaces became amenities for the people living in the building.A costly renovation that quickly found tenantsThe finished property, known as Bowtie High, began leasing in 2021. The investors had put millions of dollars into a building that had once been empty, but the apartments attracted tenants quickly. According to CNBC Make It, all 31 units were occupied within six months of the building becoming available for rent.The completed development included 27 one-bedroom apartments and four two-bedroom apartments. The homes combined features expected from newly renovated apartments with details inherited from the former school. Modern kitchens, bathrooms and other residential amenities were installed, while the original architecture helped keep the property from feeling like a completely new building. That mixture was part of the appeal. Instead of hiding the building's history, the renovation incorporated it into the finished homes.What happened to the rest of the old school?After completing Bowtie High, the investors took on another abandoned school nearby. Their next project involved the former Schwab school, which they purchased for $90,000. That building required an even more extensive renovation and was planned to become another apartment complex. The second project showed how the investors had moved from an unusual one-off idea to a broader strategy: finding old buildings that had lost their original purpose and adapting them for housing.The Bowtie High conversion, however, remains the clearest example of that approach. A property that had once been associated with classrooms, school corridors, an auditorium and a basketball court was reworked into a residential building without completely wiping away those earlier identities. The numbers also illustrate how dramatically the economics of the property changed. The investors paid $100,000 to acquire the abandoned school, then spent roughly $3.3 million on the redevelopment. After 18 months of work, the result was a 31-apartment building that was fully occupied within six months.The project is an example of adaptive reuse, in which an existing building is given a new function rather than being demolished and replaced. In this case, classrooms became homes and former school facilities became shared amenities. For the people who now live there, the building is no longer an abandoned school. But its past has not disappeared entirely. Chalkboards, high ceilings, the old gym and other surviving details continue to hint at what the property once was, even as the former classrooms serve a completely different purpose.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kavitha’s TRS to Contest in Khairtabad By-Poll
articles.summary: Telangana Rakshana Sena chief Kalvakuntla Kavitha says TRS will contest the Khairatabad bypoll, slamming Telangana govt over healthcare and education failures.
articles.body: Hyderabad: Telangana Rakshana Sena (TRS) will contest in the upcoming Khairatabad by-elections. This will be the first election by TRS after the floating the party, TRS chief Kalvakuntla Kavitha said. Kavitha said there is a need to teach a democratic lesson to those who allow cross-floor defections, which subverts the Constitution and the law.Addressing a press meet at the party office on Saturday, Kavitha came down heavily on Revanth Reddy’s govt stating that the govt is entirely incompetent and a total failure. Demanding that those who cannot manage governance step aside immediately, Kavitha announced an open war against the govt over the systemic collapse of public education and healthcare.Expressing deep anguish over the recent tragedy at RIMS Adilabad, Kavitha stated that children were charred and suffered due entirely to the apathy of the govt. Sharing official data, she highlighted the alarming toll of infant mortality across the state: 6,000 deaths in 2020–21; 4,933 deaths in 2022–23; and 3,853 deaths in 2024–25. Whichever district one looks at, nearly 200 children have lost their lives. Even in Hyderabad , which the government promised to transform into New York and Dallas, 1,046 children died last year alone, she said.Kavitha criticized the govt’s budgetary failures, pointing out that while healthcare was promised 10% of the budget, only 5% is being given. Out of ₹13,192 crores allocated last year, a mere ₹9,242 crores were spent, leaving ₹3,000 crores unspent before fresh allocations of ₹1,900 crores were made, drawing severe reprimands from the CAG. Furthermore, 7 out of 11 health schemes have been given a zero budget, Aarogyasri arrears of ₹500 crores remain pending, NIMS requires Chief Minister intervention just to secure a bed with a 7-month wait for surgeries, and Niloufer Hospital is operating at 200% bed occupancy.Announcing direct action, Kavitha stated that TRS would now visit govt hospitals in every district. She urged the public and youth to inspect local medical facilities, document conditions with photographs, and question authorities, stating, “Let us fix the situation ourselves, even if we have to skin this government alive.”Kavitha demanded that private hospitals utilizing government-allotted land must strictly enforce the mandatory 25% free treatment quota for the poor.ends/You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news. articles.title: Twice bitten, never shy: Duo arrested in publicity stunt on Maoists’ name
articles.summary: Two youths were arrested in Toopran after staging a fake Maoist letter and red flag stunt, using AI tools to boost social media views; police seized phones and a bike.
articles.body: Hyderabad: What appeared to be a late-night Maoist warning at Toopran police station and municipal office turned out to be a publicity stunt aimed at generating social media views and followers, with police arresting two youths from Nagulapalli in connection with the incident.The arrested men were identified as Banda Madhu (23) and Chintakindi Sridhar (23). Police seized a motorcycle and two mobile phones from them.Medak SP DV Srinivasa Rao said around 1:30 am on the intervening night of Tuesday, a masked man entered Toopran police station, placed a red cloth carrying a letter on the reception table and left. Another person was waiting outside on a motorcycle. A similar letter and red cloth were placed at the municipal office around the same time.The letters were purportedly issued in the name of Maoists and carried the names “Alexendar Apth” and “Ganapathi Anna”, along with sickle and hammer symbols. The contents condemned the recent death sentences awarded to 10 convicted Maoists by a special NIA court in Jagdalpur, Chhattisgarh, in the 2013 Jhiram Ghati attack case and warned of an intensified campaign against executions.Jhiram Ghati attack took place on May 25, 2013, when armed CPI (Maoist) cadres ambushed a Congress Parivartan Yatra convoy in Bastar district. Several senior Congress leaders, including Nand Kumar Patel, Mahendra Karma and Vidya Charan Shukla, were among those killed.Police registered a case after the letters were found and began analysing CCTV footage and technical evidence. The investigation was given special attention after a letter in the name of Maoists had surfaced during chief minister A Revanth Reddy’s Medaram visit early this year.The SP said a special team headed by Toopran DSP Narender Goud was formed to trace those behind the letters. “The investigation revealed that the main accused, Banda Madhu, staged the incident with the intention of gaining publicity on social media and increasing followers and views,” Srinivasa Rao said.Police revealed that Medaram incident had not generated the publicity Madhu had expected, following which he allegedly planned a similar act at Toopran.According to the investigation, Madhu used AI tools to prepare the letter and subsequently made changes to create three versions. Madhu then allegedly wore a mask and black raincoat, entered the police station and placed the letter on the reception table. He also recorded the act on his mobile phone, police said. The photographs and video were later sent to people known to him, according to the investigation.Police subsequently gathered information about the suspects’ movements and traced them to Nagulapalli. Madhu and Sridhar were arrested on Thursday night near Nagulapalli bridge.“The CCTV footage, technical evidence and information gathered during the investigation helped the special team identify the accused and establish their movements,” the SP said.Police are continuing the investigation into the incident and examining the digital material recovered from the accused.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news. articles.title: UK PM Andy Burnham’s wife quits marketing  job to focus on ‘first lady’ duties
articles.summary: Marie-France van Heel resigns from her marketing role to focus on first lady duties, supporting UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham during crucial international engagements and events.
articles.body: Marie-France van Heel, the wife of UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, has stepped down from her senior role at a Manchester electric vehicle charging company as she takes on a more active role alongside her husband.Van Heel, 56, had served as chief customer officer at Be.EV since 2024. She will remain on the company’s board in an advisory capacity, Downing Street said.Her decision comes as her schedule increasingly involves accompanying Burnham on official trips and attending events in the UK and overseas.She travelled with the Prime Minister to the United Nations General Assembly in New York earlier this week, where she met Olena Zelenska, the wife of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and Diana Carney, the spouse of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.Van Heel also attended a lunch hosted by US First Lady Melania Trump.She is understood to be building relationships with spouses of other world leaders ahead of the UK taking on the G20 presidency next year and the G7 presidency the following year.Her recent engagements have also included accompanying Burnham to the opening ceremony of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.She attended the opening of the Bayeux Tapestry, where she met King Charles and Queen Camilla, along with French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte.A Downing Street spokesman confirmed her departure from Be.EV.“Marie-France van Heel has taken the decision to step down from her position as chief customer officer at Be.EV,” the spokesman said.“She will continue to serve on the company's board in an advisory role.”The spokesman also said Burnham had already recused himself from decisions concerning EV charging.Burnham and van Heel have continued to divide their time between Downing Street and their home in Warrington since he became Prime Minister.Burnham has previously said he wants to work from No 10 North. According to the Observer, van Heel decided that continuing her Manchester-based role alongside international travel and events in London would be difficult to manage.You use AI every day. articles.title: Diana after Diana: How her story kept changing long after her death
articles.summary: Twenty-nine years ago, on August 31, 1997, a woman was ‘hunted’ to her death.
articles.body: Twenty-nine years ago, on August 31, 1997, a woman was ‘hunted’ to her death.And yet her carcass still finds its way onto paper and television screens, every few years hollowed out, stuffed and reconstructed into whatever we think it is best for her to become.Diana Frances Spencer, who later became the Princess of Wales, has lived two lives but has been only allowed to die in one of them. There is the Diana who lived, and died as the paparazzi hunted her on a fateful night on the roads of Paris. And there is a Diana we keep after her death, one we constantly remake and eulogise.She now exists as versions – a princess, a wife, a mother, a fashion icon, a beguiled lover, a kind-hearted woman, a celebrity, a victim – but did all these versions truly belong to her or do we continue to impose her with a history we create in the present?This month, Diana’s younger brother, Charles Spencer, has painted his version of his sister onto the pages of a memoir titled, ‘Swan Song: Diana, My Sister’. And in an excerpt from the book he creates a portrait of the relationship the now-King Charles shared with his first wife.According to Spencer, in the days after Diana’s death, he and the then-Prince Charles argued over whether William and Harry should walk behind their mother’s coffin. Spencer recalls Charles ending the argument with the words: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.” Buckingham Palace has disputed the recollection, saying that grief can cloud memory and affect judgement but Spencer has stood firm by his account.But is Charles right, have we forgotten Diana in her essence and replaced her with a mythologised version?To even pose this question is absurd, twenty-nine years from her death our eyes and ears still follow her. We stand pressed against the door hoping to eavesdrop onto another conversation she may have had.We cannot forget Diana given how good we have become at remembering her.Spencer remembers her as his Diana, his elder sister; the Palace has their version of her; and we, some who weren’t even born back then, have our version, constructed secondhand, through screens and pages.And in all this remembrance, the woman herself becomes harder to see.The remaking of DianaBut perhaps we should have seen this coming, Diana was being remade long before she died.Even when she was alive, the world was already busy deciding what she meant. Prescribing meaning onto her every move, making a photograph of her as a child evidence of her love for children. Her tears could become evidence of her sensitivity, her unhappiness could become a story about the woman trapped inside the institution.Diana and her story were growing alongside each other, very much in the public eye, devoid of the privacy it desired and deserved.Edward White, author of Dianaworld, describes her as a cultural “cut-and-shut” — a term borrowed from the practice of welding parts of different wrecked cars together to make something that looks whole from a distance. Diana, he argues, became a figure made up of very different, sometimes contradictory identities.Perhaps that is why there has never been just one Diana, she ended up becoming someone the public could take for themselves.Even her designers were not simply dressing a princess, they were helping construct one. Catherine Walker spoke of creating an “Arthurian Princess” for one of Diana’s Middle Eastern tours, while another dress deliberately invoked Elizabeth I. Even her image could be made to carry history, fantasy and national mythology.Diana’s ‘fairytale’ never had a textbook happy ending. She first became a princess, who won the hearts of whoever witnessed her. Then she became a victim of infidelity that supposedly stemmed from the heart of a jealous man. And all her years shaping up to be an icon, she may now have ended up becoming a reflection of herself.And eventually, the reflection starts to look more familiar than the woman herself.Diana becomes Diana jiEven in her death, Diana travelled, and as she travelled she changed. For some people in Pakistan, White wrote, she became something closer to the daughter-in-law that an Asian family might recognise. After her death, a reader writing in the Eastern Eye even imagined her as “Raj Kumari Diana ji of Southallpur”, giving the Princess of Wales an Indian honorific and, jokingly, an imaginary kingdom of her own.A woman arrives from somewhere else and, over time, becomes slightly less of the woman she was and slightly more of what the people looking at her need her to be.For some South Asian communities, Diana’s story came to carry their own tensions with family, tradition and individuality. She became the daughter-in-law who rebelled against familial expectations, young brides could identify with her. Women struggling for their own identity but adamant enough to have it, saw themselves in the Princess of Wales.But for these women she was alive, not a figure of the past. What happens when the person is gone but the story keeps travelling?Talking to TOI, Apoorva Jyoti, a young woman in her early 20s based out of Pune, shared what she felt about the late Princess. Someone so distant from the princess, in both place and time, still has pieces of her she remembers.The first words that came to her were “People’s Princess”. Then came the Diana who helped destigmatise HIV and AIDS, the Diana who worked with NGOs and charities, the Diana who cared for people at a ground level, the Diana who had a “very horrible” and “very tumultuous” marriage, the Diana who faced “a lot of patriarchy”, the Diana who was graceful, fashionable, empathetic and “very ahead of her time”.She called her an “amazing role model”, particularly for women, and described her as a “princess of dreams”, someone whose influence was remarkable precisely because she had been given a position that separated her from ordinary people and yet seemed able to reach them.And then there was the tragedy, which seemed to sit underneath all of it. Her death was “extremely tragic”, her life almost too extraordinary to have been real, more like something you would watch in a film or on television, a royal family, a disastrous marriage, a woman who became beloved by ordinary people, and then a death that made the story even harder to look away from.She had never met Diana, had not lived through the years in which Diana became Diana, and yet she had a very complete picture of her.But perhaps that picture tells us less about Diana than it does about what happens to Diana once she belongs to other people.For Apoorva, she is the woman who cared. For someone else, she may be the woman who escaped a marriage, or the woman who challenged the Palace, or the fashion icon, or the tragic heroine, or simply the princess who seemed to understand ordinary people.The pieces are all there, but Diana has become a jigsaw puzzle to the blind. The pieces fit each other, but if we could see, we would know that the picture was all wrong.This is what it means to be Diana, to never really be allowed to belong entirely to yourself, even in death. To be forced to perform for the public, while your body rests six-feet under, marked by a gravestone adorned with fresh flowers as your body wiltsWhen she was alive the cameras hunted her and in her death, we hunted for her. We become the paparazzi.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: At least 12 dead in suicide bomb blast near police post in northwestern Pakistan
articles.summary: At least 12 people were killed and around 35 others wounded on Saturday when a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at a roadside police
articles.body: At least 12 people were killed and around 35 others wounded on Saturday when a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at a roadside police checkpoint in northwestern Pakistan, police and rescue officials said.Also Read: Explosive-laden truck rams into mosque near police offices in Pakistan's Kohat; 21 deadThe attack took place in Dera Ismail Khan, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Local police chief Safdar Baloch said most of the injured were security personnel and passersby, with some in critical condition.According to Baloch, gunmen later opened fire on an ambulance carrying victims to a nearby hospital, killing a rescue worker and injuring two others.Two women and a child were also among those killed in the suicide bombing, he added.Pakistani Taliban claims responsibilityThe Pakistani Taliban, or Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack. The TTP is separate from, but allied with, the Afghan Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021 after the US withdrew its troops.Pakistan has witnessed a surge in militant attacks in recent years, many of them claimed by the TTP and the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), a separatist group primarily active in neighbouring Balochistan province.Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of allowing TTP members to operate from Afghan soil and have demanded that Kabul prevent cross-border attacks into Pakistan. Afghan authorities have denied allowing their territory to be used for attacks against other countries.Dera Ismail Khan is near South Waziristan, a former militant stronghold where the Pakistani military has carried out several operations in recent years.In December 2023, a suicide bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at the main gate of a police station in Dera Ismail Khan, killing at least 23 security personnel in one of the deadliest attacks in the area. It was claimed by Tehreek-e-Jihad Pakistan, a small militant group believed to be an offshoot of the TTP.(With AP inputs)You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Outrage as East German town bans Holocaust ‘stumbling blocks’
articles.summary: There has been outrage after a small town in eastern Germany banned the installation of new Holocaust memorial plaques that mark the last known residence or workplace of Jews and other victims of the genocide.
articles.body: There has been outrage after a small town in eastern Germany banned the installation of new Holocaust memorial plaques that mark the last known residence or workplace of Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution. ‘Stolpersteine,’ meaning ‘stumbling blocks’, are found across Germany, as well as in other European countries, and are intended as a daily reminder of Nazi atrocities. The motion was proposed by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), who argued that passersby are “walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims.” On Thursday, the city council of Heidenau, a town near Dresden in Saxony, backed the motion. The parties’ local branches instead proposed that future Holocaust commemorations should be kept at the town’s memorial site at its northern cemetery, German media report. CNN has approached both parties for comment. The move has sparked backlash, with opponents arguing that part of the purpose of the memorials is their subtle intrusion into everyday life. The small 10cm brass cubes, often installed in sidewalks outside residential homes, are the work of German artist Gunter Demnig who initiated the project in the 1990s. They all carry similar information, such as the individual’s name, date of deportation, and place of death. To date 116,000 plaques have been installed across 31 countries, the vast majority are in Germany. Demnig himself has rejected the recent motion in Heidenau. Speaking to German media, he said that the blocks must be visible in the specific locations where people used to live or work, and that they help bring history to life for young people. He said he was not surprised by the ban, given the AfD’s recent electoral successes, and said of the CDU that the party “should perhaps drop its ‘C’. Because they’ve clearly left Christianity behind.” Felix Banaszak, co-leader of Germany’s Green Party, described it as a scandal and said that the reasoning that people were stepping on the blocks was “absurd.” “They bring the names and fates of the victims into our everyday lives and prompt us to pause for a moment,” he told German media. Charlotte Knobloch, the president of a Jewish association in Bavaria and a Holocaust survivor herself, described the town council’s decision as the “completely wrong path.” Speaking to Germany’s Funke Media Group, she said that while she herself was not a friend of the ‘Stolpersteine’ concept, “decentralized commemoration that is not banished from public spaces” is key for the country’s culture of remembrance. The AfD has long challenged Germany’s forms of commemoration of the atrocities committed under Adolf Hitler. In Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD recently sealed it best-ever win in state elections, a prominent AfD official described their vision to overhaul the state’s school history lessons as “more Bismark – less Hitler.” On a federal level, the party was designated as a far-right extremist organization by German domestic intelligence, although that designation is currently under review. Individuals within the party have also been accused of being extremists. Aside from the fact that a far-right policy has been approved at the local level in Germany, the move lays bare a growing issue in German politics; adherence to the ‘Brandmauer,’ or firewall, an informal position for mainstream parties that sees them rule out cooperation with the AfD. This firewall, which is designed to keep the far right out of political decision making and stifle their growth, is under serious pressure. The CDU’s willingness to work together with the AfD to pass this motion has sparked criticism of the CDU leadership and comes at a time when the Chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz is already facing a crisis over poor performances in recent regional elections. The International Auschwitz Committee slammed the CDU’s support of the motion as scandalous, according to Deutsche Welle. “This is a transparent and despicable attempt to drive Nazi victims in Heidenau out of the city once again and dispose of them where, according to the AfD, their memory has belonged a long time ago — at the cemetery,” the committee’s executive vice president said.

On September 24, 2026, the city council of the Saxon city approved a motion to that effect, proposed by the AfD and CDU, by a majority vote. articles.title: Brazil’s Lula bans online betting as re-election race tightens
articles.summary: SAO PAULO — Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday announced a ban on online betting operations in Latin America’s largest economy ⁠and unveiled a new debt relief program aimed at households, the latest in a series of measures introduced ahead of next month’s election.
articles.body: SAO PAULO — Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday announced a ban on online betting operations in Latin America’s largest economy ⁠and unveiled a new debt relief program aimed at households, the latest in a series of measures introduced ahead of next month’s election. Opinion polls have shown Lula locked in a tight race with right-wing Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, ahead of the Oct. 4 first-round vote. The executive order bans online betting operations in Brazil, less than two years after the government kicked off a legal framework allowing the industry to operate. It takes immediate effect but ⁠must be approved by Congress within 120 days to remain in force. The crackdown ​reflects ⁠growing concern within the government that rising spending on gambling has drained household budgets and contributed to record levels of indebtedness. Recent surveys showed roughly three-quarters of Brazilians support a complete ban on online betting. “We are facing a public health issue involving ⁠online betting. It is a serious problem,” said Finance Minister Dario Durigan during the announcement. Durigan said that betting firms’ websites will remain available ​for users to ⁠claim remaining funds until Oct. 5. App stores and ‌network providers will be required to block these websites on Oct. 6, he added. Flavio Bolsonaro called the measure “populist, hypocritical and politically motivated” during a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday. Online betting was legalized in Brazil in 2018 under then-President Michel Temer but remained ‌largely unregulated throughout Jair Bolsonaro’s administration. Lula signed legislation in 2023 establishing rules and explicitly authorizing ‌online casino games in addition to sports betting. Licensed operators have been allowed to offer services nationwide since January 2025 after paying concession fees and meeting regulatory requirements. Officials have argued that betting losses have fueled public dissatisfaction with the economy, despite record-low unemployment and relatively subdued inflation in the country. The Finance Ministry estimates Brazilian households spend around 60 billion reais ($11.57 billion) ⁠annually on online betting, generating roughly 10 billion reais in tax revenue. JPMorgan said listed companies most exposed to Brazil include Evolution, which derives about 9% of sales from the country, Allwyn, whose Betano business contributes 6% to 7% of EBITDA, Entain and Flutter. ANJL, an association representing the betting sector, said in a statement that the measure would push more than 30 million gamblers into illegal websites, adding it disrespects investments made in compliance with the law. Debt release program Lula also announced a new initiative aimed at reducing the burden of household debt, only months after relaunching a broad federally backed consumer debt renegotiation program known as “Desenrola,” which was unveiled in 2023. The government said it will hold an auction ‌in November to buy and restructure household debt, spending 15 billion reais ($2.9 billion) to acquire up to 150 billion reais ($29 billion) of ​delinquent loans at discounts of at least 90%. The program is expected to cover about half of the debt stock deemed ‌eligible. Households would then be able to clear overdue obligations at the ⁠discounted value, with the full benefit of the write-down passed through to borrowers. The initiative targets debts that have been ⁠overdue for two to 4.5 years, mainly credit card balances and unsecured personal loans. Planning Minister Bruno Moretti said the auction will cover debts of up to 10,000 reais ($2,000). “This is a ‌better Desenrola than the previous versions,” Lula ​said. “In the earlier Desenrola, people had to approach banks individually. Now the ‌government will purchase the debt and settle it on behalf of ​borrowers.” The measure had already been flagged by the government last week as part of Lula’s election-year economic agenda.
