articles.title: Third suspect arrested in death of Mississippi woman found hanging at ‘staged’ crime scene
articles.summary: A third person has been arrested in the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old woman who police said was found hanging from a tree behind an abandoned Mississippi home in August.
articles.body: A third person has been arrested in the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old woman who police said was found hanging from a tree behind an abandoned Mississippi home in August. Eric Clark, 45, surrendered to police on Friday and is charged with murder. Police also disclosed on Friday that according to an autopsy investigation, “the scene and the hanging were staged.” No other details were released about the scene or Fortune’s killing. Clark is expected to appear in court on Monday. Two other people, Earnest Lloyd Jr. and Jarques Ratliff, were also arrested and charged with murder in connection with her death. Both men are Black. Police have released very little information about what led up to Fortune’s death. Detectives investigating the case have interviewed as many as 15 people, collected forensic evidence and followed numerous leads, police said in a news release. Authorities said Ratliff, 51, had an “association” with Fortune but did not release further details. Lloyd, 25, allegedly had a physical altercation with Fortune either days or minutes before she died, according to NBC affiliate WLBT of Jackson. Police accused Lloyd of hanging Fortune with a black cable cord, WLBT reported. Ratliff, who pleaded not guilty, and Lloyd were denied bond at separate court hearings.

articles.title: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
articles.summary: An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country.
articles.body: An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country. Video showed Maricarmen Abascal, who is a wheelchair user, being taken out of the building in the Spanish capital’s Retiro neighborhood on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance. Hundreds of supporters had gathered outside the building overnight to protest her eviction, with dozens of police officers holding them back as some tried to stop the eviction from going ahead. In a social media video posted Friday by the Madrid tenants union, Abascal gave thanks for the support she had received. Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, described the force used in the eviction as “completely disproportionate and unnecessary” and decried the intransigence of the building’s owners. The case has brought new attention to an ongoing housing crisis in major cities across Spain, as gentrification has caused rents to skyrocket and the stock of affordable housing to shrink, leading to growing public anger. Tenants unions and other housing groups on Thursday held protests and rallies in 16 cities, including Granada, Logroño and Zaragoza. The Madrid tenants union plans to hold another major protest in the capital Saturday evening. An investment fund acquired Abascal’s building in 2018 and sought a steep increase in her rent, and she had been fighting eviction for more than five years, according to the Madrid tenants union. Duro said court officials and representatives of the fund, Urbagestión, had refused to suspend the eviction despite a pending court filing, humanitarian appeals and evidence that public authorities were working to secure alternative accommodation. “They’re all inhumane,” Abascal said in a Spanish television interview the day before her eviction. “It’s as if I’m living with a machete at the back of my neck, ready to be chopped off at any moment.” Duro also said an anonymous individual had offered to cover the rent payments, but the landlord declined to sign a new lease. “We’ve been trying to negotiate with the landlords right up until the last moment, and they’ve flatly refused everything,” she said, decrying “a lack of humanity” in her treatment and “all these public resources” channeled into enabling the eviction. Urbagestión did not respond to a request for comment. The fresh wave of anger comes after protests in recent years against overtourism in Barcelona, where activists say a surge in apartments being used for short-term vacation rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing. The European Union announced new rules earlier this month aimed at tackling the housing crunch caused by short-term rentals in tourism hot spots. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the eviction as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept either as a country or, of course, from the perspective of public institutions.” Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Sánchez accused Madrid’s conservative regional government of pursuing luxury penthouses while ignoring demand for social housing. Irene Hernández López, a 31-year-old test engineer living and renting in Chamberí, about 2 miles from Retiro, said what had happened to Abascal was “outrageous,” and she is worried similar evictions were already happening to other tenants around the city. “Housing has become a product that people do business with,” she told NBC News. “It no longer matters that it’s your personal world, where you live and where you do your life.” Hernández López, who pays 500 euros ($570) for a room in an apartment she shares with two others, said she was currently looking to move because the property was old and needs repairs, but that the rental market in Madrid was “terrible,” with prices “rising extremely quickly” and very little available. “Some rooms are 500 euros or 600 euros and you think, ‘How am I supposed to live here? How can I pay 500 euros for this?’” she said. “I do think prices should be regulated, because wages aren’t going up while housing prices keep increasing. I don’t know how we’re supposed to keep going.” Dan Nicander, secretary-general for the International Union of Tenants, said the situation in Spain was something his organization had seen in many countries in Europe. “It’s a part of the financialization problem, seeing housing as an asset more than a home to people,” he told NBC News. It’s “really tough” for the people living in the houses to do anything about it, he added, saying the responsibility lay with politicians “to regulate the market in a way that it shouldn’t be that easy to buy and invest and then not [be] using the houses as homes.” “Housing is a right,” he said. “It’s a fundamental right, first and foremost. It shouldn’t be a commodity.”

articles.title: Trump rejects Iran’s latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump said Saturday that he rejects Iran’s latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, adding that it is unacceptable.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Saturday rejected Iran’s latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, calling it “unacceptable.” Iran’s top diplomat, Abbas Araghchi, announced earlier this week that Tehran had submitted a fresh offer to the United States that would see the critical waterway reopen and negotiations resume between the two nations, in exchange for the US meeting several long-standing demands. The Iranian foreign minister did not elaborate on the exact conditions but said they were “nothing more” than what was included in the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding, which was signed in June but collapsed shortly after amid renewed fighting. That initial agreement included provisions on sanctions relief; the release of frozen assets; and a cessation of military operations, including in Lebanon. But Trump poured cold water on Iran’s latest proposal on Saturday. “I reject their proposal,” the US president said when asked by reporters what he thought about Iran’s plan. “They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” he added. “They want a make a deal, and I think that’s fine. I like making a deal too, but that deal would not be acceptable.” The proposal would have begun “as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” Araghchi said Friday. “If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States,” Araghchi told reporters during a visit to New York for this week’s United Nations General Assembly. “You cannot bomb a country, threaten its annihilation, impose a maritime blockade, and coercive measures, and expect automatic restoration of security and navigation,” Araghchi added. ‘We are not in a rush’ In response to Araghchi’s comments, a White House official previously told CNN they were having “positive and constructive discussions through the mediators.” “The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush,” the official said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio struck a similar tone earlier this week, saying, “If there’s going to be a deal with Iran…it’s going to involve a lot of hard work over a period of time.” The Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported on Friday that Trump told staff that a renewed bombing campaign is likely after the upcoming midterm elections. The officials were reported as saying Trump’s views could change over the coming weeks. CNN has reached out to the White House for comment on the report. This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Tehran submitted a proposal via Qatar to reopen the strait and resume nuclear talks within a week if Washington agreed.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has rejected a roadmap submitted by Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz within a week.

“I reject their proposal,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday, before departing for Tennessee by helicopter.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday that Tehran formally submitted a seven-day roadmap to the US via mediator Qatar, and was awaiting Washington’s response.

“It appears as though the proposal is dead in the water,” said Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC.

Late on Friday, US media reports indicated Trump would reject the proposal .

Trump was “privately sceptical” that Tehran would meet his demands, and reportedly told aides that he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the November US midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, quoting unnamed US officials.

“President Trump has vacillated between extreme optimism, saying that ‘talks are going well’ to ‘I want to annihilate Iran’,” Hanna said about the recent diplomacy between Washington and Tehran.

“There is no consistency in terms of the [Trump] administration’s reaction,” he said.

But “the one thing that has been made clear by President Trump is that he is content to stay in the status of limbo”, Hanna added, despite concerns from much of the American public that the Iran conflict is turning into another “never-ending war”.

The Strait of Hormuz, a waterway key to the world’s oil supply, is central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which is at an impasse after nearly seven months, though new mediation efforts took place this week.

Earlier in the week, Araghchi held talks with Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital shipping channel.

On Friday, the top Iranian diplomat said: “Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days.”

He was speaking at the United Nations in New York, where he and other senior Iranian officials were attending the General Assembly.

Under the plan, Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observe a ceasefire covering the region, including Lebanon and Yemen.

“The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure,” Araghchi had said.

On Saturday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera that Tehran no longer trusts negotiations with the US after previous rounds of talks were followed by attacks and sanctions.

“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” said Pezeshkian, who was also in New York for the UNGA.

He denied that Iran was responsible for blocking the Strait of Hormuz, saying the US “closed the routes before us”. He described the closure as “a natural response when routes are cut off to Iran”.

The Iranian president said the crisis could be resolved through negotiations rather than force, and that the waterway would reopen to commercial shipping if talks ended the war.

articles.title: Shocking revelation in Mississippi Black woman's death: Tasia Fortune was killed before body was hung from tree, police say; drug dispute suspected

articles.body: Tasia Fortune, a Black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree behind an abandoned home in Jackson last month, had already died before her body was placed there, a police detective testified in court Friday. Jackson police detective Samuel Dukes told a hearing that the hanging appeared to have been “staged”, citing the medical examiner's opinion. Authorities have ruled Fortune's death a homicide but have not publicly disclosed the exact cause of death or explained why her body was hung from the tree.Fortune's body was discovered on August 3. The circumstances drew widespread attention because the scene evoked the history of lynchings and racial violence in Mississippi.According to Dukes, investigators believe the killing was linked to a dispute involving drugs. He testified that interviews with people familiar with the case indicated Fortune fought her attackers before she was killed.Two arrested in murder casePolice have arrested two men in connection with Fortune's death and issued a warrant for a third person.Jarques Ratliff, 51, was the first suspect arrested and has pleaded not guilty. He remains in the Hinds County jail without bond. Ratliff's preliminary hearing is aimed at determining whether prosecutors have sufficient evidence to send the case to a grand jury for possible indictment. The hearing is scheduled to resume on September 30.Police also arrested 25-year-old Earnest Lloyd Jr this week. Both men face murder charges.During Friday's hearing, Ratliff said Fortune had been his friend.Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, told reporters outside court that she knew her daughter had died before her body was hung. She said what troubled her was learning that Fortune had fought for her life.“I know she did. I know my daughter,” Spivey said, according to AP.Who was Tasia Fortune?Fortune was a mother of four who had struggled with homelessness in recent years, according to her mother. Spivey said she was unsure where her daughter had been living when she died.She said Fortune had been trying to rebuild her life and had spoken about starting a cleaning business.The investigation remains ongoing. articles.title: EC probes claim of Rajmahal voter being listed in Bangladesh electoral records
articles.summary: EC probes claim that a Rajmahal voter is also listed in Bangladesh electoral rolls; notice issued, verification ongoing, possible deletion before Oct 19 roll.
articles.body: Ranchi: A complaint filed before the Election Commission has alleged that a voter enrolled in Jharkhand’s Rajmahal assembly constituency is the same person whose details appear in Bangladesh’s electoral records under another name. The allegation is being examined by election authorities.The complaint names the voter as Atur Sheikh, also recorded as Atur Sekh, and claims he is listed in Part 372, Serial No. 51 of the electoral roll for Paschim Pranpur in Sahibganj district. It includes copies of the Jharkhand electoral roll and documents claimed to be from Bangladesh’s electoral records, where a voter named Md Ataur Rahman is listed.Chief electoral officer K Ravi Kumar said the complaint was received about a month ago and that a notice had been issued to the voter. “He has not appeared before the election authorities. During field verification, officials found that he was not living at the Rajmahal address,” Kumar said.Officials said the voter’s wife told the verification team that he works in Mumbai. Kumar said the woman’s electoral status was also being examined.“If the couple fails to produce the required documents, their names could be deleted from the final electoral roll,” he said. The final roll is scheduled to be published on Oct19 after the ongoing Special Intensive Revision.The electoral registration officer is examining whether the voter fulfils the requirements of Indian citizenship, being at least 18 years old and ordinarily residing in the polling area.Kumar said the ERO would pass a reasoned order after examining the evidence. He also said there was no provision for referring the matter to Bangladesh’s Election Commission.The complaint claims that Bangladesh records show Md Ataur Rahman, born on Jan 1, 1970, as the son of Md Azar Ali and Amena Begum. It alleges that he later secured enrolment in the Indian electoral roll using forged documents.The complainant has sought verification of the voter’s identity and documents, deletion of the electoral entry if the allegations are proved, and action against those responsible. The complaint also refers to cases in Radhanagar and Barharwa police stations. The relevance of these cases to the complaint has not yet been established.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. articles.title: Kern County detective determined to find out what happened to Ada Kaplan Moore in California 15 years ago
articles.summary: On March 29, 2011, the body of Ada Kaplan Moore was found on the grounds of an orchard in Arvin, California. She had been decapitated. The Kern County Sheriff’s Office is investigating her case.
articles.body: For more than half a century, homicide investigators have gathered annually at the California Homicide Investigators Association (CHIA) Conference. “They have a conference and talk about -- kind of case studies on how they were able to solve a homicide investigation,” Detective Ashley Thompson of the Kern County Sheriff’s Office told Dateline. At this year’s conference, Thompson met some of the Dateline team and told them about a cold case she’s working on: the unsolved homicide of Ada Kaplan Moore. On the morning of March 29, 2011, the body of an unidentified woman was found by employees on the grounds of an Arvin, California, orchard. The Kern County Sheriff’s Office responded to the scene that day. “Kern County is -- is pretty rural,” Thompson said. “And in 2011 in that area, it was one hundred percent rural.” The woman had been decapitated. “That definitely took me aback,” Thompson said. The death was ruled a homicide. Nothing else of note was found nearby, which led investigators to believe the orchard was not the crime scene. “We were able to pretty much determine that she was probably just placed there,” she said. Authorities were unable to identify the woman. “She just wasn’t in the system,” Thompson said. She was a Jane Doe for more than a decade. That changed in 2023. “Forensic investigative genetic genealogy was something that helped us identify her,” Thompson said. The victim was identified as 64-year-old Ada Kaplan Moore. After Ada was identified, Thompson was assigned to the case to investigate her homicide. The detective’s first order of business? “Try to find anybody who knew her,” Thompson said. “I was able to find very [few] people.” She was able to speak with Ada’s husband. “I was given information that she had left this relationship, and that was pretty much it,” she said. “The information I got about her is very -- very little to none, to be honest.” Thompson learned Ada was not from Kern County but from the Canyon Country neighborhood of Santa Clarita in Los Angeles County, about an hour and a half from Arvin. The detective has not found any ties Ada may have had to the area where her remains were found. She learned Ada did not work and was not reported missing in 2011. “I can’t find family members that actually spent time with her, that -- that knew her. She doesn’t have any children,” Thompson said. “She doesn’t have any friends that I could find.” That’s why Thompson is trying to bring attention to Ada’s story: “To see if somebody can even recognize her,” she said. “It’s very hard to find out who she was because she was very alone.” Thompson is hoping to piece together a picture of Ada’s life and the people who knew her. “I’m really just looking for anybody who’s ever had an interaction with her that remembers her, and remembers who she was, or anything about her,” she said. Then, she hopes, she’ll be able to figure out what happened to Ada. Thompson told Dateline it bothers her that no one seems to care about Ada. “I get phone calls from loved ones all the time asking me about updates,” she said. “I don’t receive any phone calls for Ada. Nobody’s -- nobody is fighting for her.” So Detective Thompson is. “It’s a big, big case for me that I just -- I want to be able to just solve,” she said. “Because if I don’t solve it, I don’t think anybody’s gonna care.” If you have any information about Ada’s case, please call Det. Thompson’s direct line at the Kern County Sheriff’s Office at 661-391-7593. If she doesn’t answer, please leave a voicemail with contact information. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: At least 10 people killed in Russian and Ukrainian attacks
articles.summary: New strikes come after the US proposes a fresh round of Russia-Ukraine ceasefire talks in the UAE.
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine have traded attacks that have killed at least 10 people as the United States pushes for talks to end the war.

Russian attacks killed four people in Ukraine, while Ukrainian strikes killed six in Russia and Russian-occupied territory, officials on both sides said on Saturday.

In Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia, two women died under the rubble of their home, following an overnight Russian barrage of drones and missiles, the regional military administration said.

A separate Russian attack killed two people in the city of Sumy, according to local officials.

“It is essential that our partners not forget: Russia is escalating every single day,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X on Saturday.

“If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further.”

Ukraine has pressed on with long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries and industrial sites.

In Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, a Ukrainian drone attack killed three people and wounded two, with Governor Veniamin Kondratyev writing on Telegram that it had also sparked fires at two industrial facilities.

Russian media later said an oil refinery was among the targets.

Moscow-installed regional head Yevgeny Balitsky said Ukrainian strikes overnight into Saturday killed three people in the Russian-occupied part of Zaporizhzhia region, according to Russian state media.

Russia’s Defence Ministry meanwhile said Russian forces struck a cargo ⁠vessel with ⁠military supplies near Ukraine’s Black ‌Sea port of Odesa on ⁠Saturday. A logistics hub ⁠was also hit ⁠in Odesa, ⁠it ⁠added.

On Friday, Russian strikes on Kyiv killed seven people , injured 58 and forced a halt to production at Ukraine’s largest steelmaker.

ArcelorMittal said on Friday that a number of strikes in recent days had killed five workers and badly damaged one of their sites. Ukraine’s steel industry previously made up 15 percent of the country’s exports.

Ukrainian forces, for their part, hit oil refineries in Russia’s Perm and Novoshakhtinsk on Friday, causing a temporary halt to operations.

The deadly strikes came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday that Washington had proposed a meeting of Russian, Ukrainian and US officials in the United Arab Emirates.

“We are awaiting a proposal from the United States regarding the date, and the United States has suggested the Emirates as a possible location,” he said in a WhatsApp briefing.

He also said Egypt, India, Turkiye and representatives from the Middle East were taking part in talks on unblocking shipping in the Black Sea, while other nations had put forward proposals.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday that every settlement proposal remained on the table, though Moscow was still weighing what served its interests, according to Russian news agencies.

He said Moscow was prepared to return to talks with Kyiv following last week’s parliamentary elections, but accused Ukraine of trying to strike the capital and attacking polling stations.

Meanwhile, Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addressed the United Nations General Assembly on Saturday, and accused Europe of hindering talks with Ukraine.

“Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the [Donald] Trump administration is interested,” he said, referring to the US government.
